introduction: On this Sunday, God sends Ezekiel to a stubborn people, whether they listen or not. In the Gospel, Jesus is rejected in his own hometown of Nazareth, and he marvels at their lack of faith. Paul learns that God's grace is enough, for power is made perfect in weakness. Let us welcome Christ when he comes to us in ordinary people and ordinary places.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, God's grace is enough for us. Let us bring him our prayers with trust.
intentions: For the Church: that she may speak God's word with courage, whether people listen or refuse. Let us pray to the Lord.
For prophets of our time, and all who speak the truth at a cost: that God may strengthen them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who live with chronic illness, disability or weakness: that they may know that God's power is at work in them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For families and hometowns where faith has grown cold: that Christ may be welcomed there again. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may recognize Jesus in the familiar people around us. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, your power is made perfect in weakness. Give us faith to welcome your Son and courage to bear witness to him. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: My grace is sufficient for you
reflection.body:
God does not promise Ezekiel success. He sends him to a people who are "impudent and stiff-hearted" and tells him to speak "whether they will hear, or whether they will refuse." The prophet's task is to be faithful, not to be popular: "they will know that there has been a prophet among them."

In the Gospel, Jesus comes home to Nazareth. At first the people are impressed, but then they start to ask questions: "Isn't this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" They know him too well, or think they do, and "they were offended at him." Jesus says, "A prophet is not without honor, except in his own country, and among his own relatives, and in his own house." Mark adds a striking line: "He could do no mighty work there," except heal a few sick people, and "He marveled because of their unbelief."

Familiarity can blind us. We may think we already know Jesus, or that God could never speak through the ordinary people around us: a family member, a neighbor, a priest we have known for years.

Paul speaks honestly about his own weakness. He calls it "a thorn in the flesh," and he begged three times to be freed from it. The answer he received was not what he asked for: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness." So Paul concludes, "For when I am weak, then am I strong."

We often think God can only use us when we are strong. Paul learned the opposite. This week, bring to God the weakness you most wish you did not have, and ask for the grace to trust him in it. And listen for his voice in someone you might normally overlook.
